chunks: From him (Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Warraq), from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hafs ibn Suqat, from Al-Husayn ibn al-Mundhir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said: 'A man comes to me seeking credit (for goods), so I buy the merchandise on his behalf, then I sell it to him, and then I buy it back from him for my own place.' He said: 'If he has the option (to accept or reject the terms), if he wishes he sells, and if he wishes he does not sell; and you have the option, if you wish you buy, and if you wish you do not buy, so there is no harm.'

I said: 'Indeed, the people of the mosque claim that this is invalid, and they say that if he brings it back after four months, it becomes valid.' He said: 'This is merely delaying and advancing (time), so there is no harm.'

key_terms.الْخِيَار: Option/Right to choose (accept or reject a contract)
key_terms.الْعِينَةَ: Credit or buying goods on credit for someone else
key_terms.تَقْدِيمٌ وَتَأْخِيرٌ: Delaying and advancing (referring to time periods in contracts)

ai.seo_question: Is the practice of buying goods for a customer on credit and then repurchasing them from them valid in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates the practice of *istisna'* or credit-based trade by emphasizing the mutual option (*khiyar*) of both buyer and seller, thereby refuting the view that such transactions are inherently invalid without a fixed delay. He clarifies that the four-month period cited by others is merely a matter of timing (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) rather than a condition for validity, highlighting the flexibility in commercial jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly principle that commercial contracts are valid based on the consent and option of the parties, provided there is no explicit prohibition, distinguishing it from the stricter conditions often applied in other schools of thought regarding *bay' al-kali' bil-kali'*.
